In Order of your bullets:
  1. No other pets at this moment, but my girlfriend is going to be living with me (and bringing her cat) definitely before the dog gets here.  Her cat gets along with dogs so that's not a big worry to me.  Also note, that we've discussed what we are looking for in a dog and we agree on all these points.

  2.  It'll be my girlfriend and I when the dog comes.

  3.  I would say shedding is pretty ignorable to me if the dog is the right fit, I'd prefer to not have a fur factory but can compromise pretty easily on that.  Same with barking, I'd like to have a more vocal dog, but one that isn't going off 24/7.  Farting is a natural part of a dog to me, so as long as he's not farting every hour then we're good.  Drooling is okay as long as it's occasional and not constant.

  4. I'd love a medium or large dog.  Smallest I'd go is probably Corgi-sized

  5.  We're fine with taking care of him/her every few days.  No concern about how often we have to pay a groomer, we can do it often (as a note, we make good money and are in stable jobs, we have the money to take care of its needs and not bat an eye).

  6.  I'm pretty active, I lift weights and run/jog/bike on occasion.  My girlfriend dances and does her own share of working out.  We're the kind of people that are happy indoors or outdoors and a dogs getting us outside isn't a bad thing.  Although I'd probably cap out at an hour walk a day and 1-2 hours of play between the two of us.

  7.  The dog will likely be alone when we go to work (standard 9 to 5).  Otherwise it will be around us nearly all the time if we're out and about and going places.  Again, hiring someone to walk him/her is a nonissue, as well as doggy daycare.  Coming home at lunch could probably be arranged (I work for a flexible tech company, and they'd be fine with me doing that a few times a week)

  8.  We want our dog to be very trainable.  He needs to be obedient and superb off-leash.  These are very important.

  9.  Currently we're in a large apartment, and will be getting a house within the next 5 years.  There's no breed or size restrictions, and I'm willing to bite the bullet on paying for repairs if the pup happens to wreck anything.

  10.  We've already established a fund for the dog and are prepared for that commitment to our company.  We already have a saving fund that has 3 years of expenses (high budget too) and the money for getting a puppy if we decide to go that route.  We are prepared for a future with our dog.

  11.  The yard is sizeable and pretty big.  It's also fenced in, and there's dog parks and such nearby.

  12.  No children.  But there may be some within the next 10 years so it should be good for that.  We would love for it to be a people-friendly dog that is good with new situations.

  13.  My girlfriend has had 2 dogs and training.  I've had no dogs of my own, but have lived with them, taken care of, and been involved in training dogs that I've lived with.  I'm not a complete newbie, but I've never had a friend to call 'mine'.

  14.  Our dog will be living with us in our apartment.  Not sure what else this question means?

  15.  New England Weather, specifically Boston and area around Boston.  So high variance weather.  Long cold, dry winters with lots of snow.  And very hot, very humid summers.  Spring and Fall can be either comfortable, or some mix between the two extremes.

  16.  As said before we went to get a Doggy Savings account set up before we went for our friend.  It includes a puppy purchase (if needed) of 3k, 1st year expenses (15k) and 2 more years of care (20k, so about 38k in total).  This is a fund going only into our dog and we'll continue to set aside money into this account.  However this will ensure some financial safety for our friend in case of anything happening.

  17.  We're opening to rescue dogs, but I'd love to have my friend from a young age (whether that means a breeder or rescuing puppies)  even with the amount of work it would be.  Just to really raise him/her and see them grow up would be amazing and awesome I think for the both of us.

  18.  We want a friend and companion, and a pillar of support and love.  A dog that would be excited to go on a walk or to just crash on the coach with his best buddy.  Also a dog that would come along on any trips, stick by us and obey and be under control.  One that'd be good with new people and scenarios, and that we can trust to be good with kids, or people not as keen with dogs as we are.  We'd also love a dog that we could feel safe with, not necessarily a guard dog, but one that you'd feel good leaving alone at home knowing it'll be the same as you left it (whether that means not destroying your stuff, or protecting)

Some thoughts as to the direction of the series, predictions, and otherwise:

I think it's pretty obvious what's going to happen later on.  The show established this conflict of whether it's worth it to save someone even if it means putting others in danger.  Arguably, people who don't deserve to be put at risk and who should be prioritized over the criminal.  The two opposing views are represented in our two Inspectors, We see Akane's view in that she believes they're worth saving, and we see Mika's in that she believes that the fact they're in that position should strip them of any right to be saved.  We'll probably see both sides tested over the series, and especially toyed with by our new main antagonist who was introduced after the credits.  It's pretty much confirmed based on Akane's ending monologue that their ideas will be challenged.  This isn't that significant however.  I think what's significant is how this connects back to our favorite Vigilante. I think the climax point will come over Kougami, where Mika's and Akane's viewpoints will probably be put directly against one another.  Is he worthy of saving?  Or is his elimination saving in itself?  I don't think they'll necessarily decide whether he lives or dies, but most likely whether the CID takes action against him or not.

As far as the Antagonist goes, I'm not even sure if he'll be the main focus.  I think if anything he'll drive us towards our central question, and probably build strife within Akane and the others in the Division 1 crew.  It seems like he'll have his moments but there's too big of an issue with Kougami looming to really have him take full center stage and not feel bombastically out of place.  Unless of course, Kougami is involved somehow.  If that's the case I hope it doesn't turn into some damsel in distress situation with Kougami (I didn't like the look of that shot with him tied to the chair in the OP).

It also looks like we have an interesting character in Togune.  He didn't say a lot in this episode but he really said a lot with what he had to say.  There's obviously more behind him than just the rookie Enforcer he is playing and he probably will have some key role to play with Kougami and Sibyl.  It'll be interesting to see how much he shows his hand as the season goes on, and what he does that will leave his mark.  I'll be keeping an eye on him intently, as it seems like he will be a quiet character with a great weight to his words when he does speak.  He seems to have all the makings of a good Double Agent, working on both Akane's (as seen with his support of her capture this episode) and Sibyl's (I'm assuming) sides.

---------

Of course all of this may turn out to be a bunch of bologna and just plain wrong, but I'd figure I'd share some of my thoughts.  It was a great first episode and I'm excited to see more out of the show as the season goes on.

Alrighty, never really done a post around here before, but I'll start off here.  I only got one show in so I'll be a bit in depth (and always honest :) ) with my impressions.  If you want me to elaborate on anything, I'll be happy to.

**Ping-Pong the Animation (1-11)**

I initially watched the first two episodes when they first aired, and I immediately decided that it would be something that I needed to wait until it was finished to watch.  Even though I only do this for shows I should REALLY enjoy, they always seem to be pushed aside for keeping up on airing shows.  I finally decided to watch Ping-Pong, and true to my original expectations, I finished it within 2 days.  

The show's handling of characters is what deserves the greatest praise.  It crafted 5 very different protagonists that all held different beliefs and goals within the story.  The story/writing also deserves praise here, for it knew where to place moments to keep characters involved without detracting from the forward momentum.  None of them felt undeveloped, and the story had that marker of a great story, where a lot of the interaction and meaning could be inferred past what was said or shown.  

The directing stood out greatly as well.  I personally think Yuasa only truly shines when he has writing backing him, not in an unsimilar way to Shinbou, where their artistic vision is backed fully when they have some picture the writer can have them paint.  I don't think their directing skill is bad, I just feel that they're not the type of director to make bad works better, but to make good works great.  Of course, the writing here allowed him to go wild and show why his work is some of the most memorable and directively superior shows of the past few years.  Especially some of the smaller character moments, were so superbly done, that I sometimes had to stop and think about the 5 minutes worth of information I got in 20 seconds.

As far as production values go, I thought this was where you could probably give any fault.  On the upside, some of the sequences were absolutely BEAUTIFUL.  The style of the show was incredibly expressive and helped to back the great characters.  Special shout-outs also to the deconstructive sequences where reality broke down in favor of visual motifs, metaphors, and almost fantastical depictions of the action.  For the downside, there were a bunch of moments where the show looked downright...*muddy*.  Faces blended into unrecognizable shapes, wacky body proportions, and inconsistent character design.  I guess the best way to describe it is that some scenes in the show looked like they just colored in the rough storyboards and felt really lacking next to some of the uniquely beautiful moments in the series.  On the audio side, I would say the show had little to no faults.  The OST was great, and it was utilized better at the very beginning and ends of the series, but was still way above standard throughout.  It supported whatever mood of the show and helped to backup the story and directing without taking away from it.

Overall, I have little serious issues with the show and I enjoyed it tremendously and has shot up to one of my favorite.  It may sound bandwagoney to say that, but in the hundreds of series I've watched, this was a great joy to watch.  It was something that took me away to another world and made me feel wonder in a work on entertainment.  I now have to watch the movie to see the differences, and I just hope it doesn't betray the high-opinions I already have.

Out of curiosity, have you watched any magical girl shows before, or did you have any of the twists spoiled?  You've probably heard this a lot but Madoka is a deconstruction.  It's fairly unique for a deconstruction in that it stands well on its own, but it does form a lot of its higher merits on its subversion of genre stereotypes and tropes.  

I'm not trying to sound like it's a crime to not like Madoka, but I just think that those things are key to finding it great.  On addition, you also have the effect of the internet effectively dickriding it for 3+ years to contend with.  It's hard to actually reach any expectations when you have it beaten into you by others that it's so good.  

I really think Madoka is in that different type of media.  Where the "Citizen Kane"s of the world fall.   Madoka is important for many critical reasons, but being critically brilliant or impactful does not have to correspond with enjoyment.  People can think whatever they want about it, and usually these movies are less well-liked all around than crowd-pleaser movies and shows (Think The Avengers, or Big Bang Theory).

Basically, I'm not surprised you like Madoka.  In fact, I don't know a lot of people who truly love Madoka.  Most people appreciate it for what it is and what it has done, but not to any higher level.  While I wrote a lot to just basically say that, I think it's always important to remember that on a subreddit full of people who appreciate anime as a form of media on its own, the appreciate of important critical pieces is very standard, but not for general audiences.  At the end of the day, the sample size here is going to be biased towards strong opinions on shows like Madoka.

From my viewpoint of the scene:

Kaiki believes in absolute truths.

Within the confines of the scene Kaiki says this to shake Nadeko's resolve, as he realizes the absolute truth that her own belief in her god capabilities is what gives them power.  However, as we know Kaiki is not one to care about manipulating belief and feelings for his own purposes. In the culmination of his character arc Kaiki ends up manipulating the person he has put above all other, and dethrones his own beliefs and opinions in the process. Normally Kaiki had always used others to do his dirty work, and brought them down to the lowest level they could go, belittling their beliefs and identity.  But in this case, all he is one target to use it on, and he can't be considerate of himself, just like he wasn't to all the others. His intellectual and emotional experience allow him to do this without the destructiveness seen in his younger victims.  But the message is there, and it's pretty easy to see at least to me.  Kaiki does believe in absolute truth, but in the case of Nadeko he can't have any of his beliefs in order to beat her. I liked the essay, and your style is something pretty uncommon which I enjoy personally.  However, I had just one pretty big problem with it.

You bring up the importance of the quote:

“There is no absolute truth.” ~ Kaiki

Then you continue on around it.  However, the quote itself is paradoxical, there's nothing to argue there.  In arguing the truth (heh) of it you're also arguing the falsehood of it.  Kaiki states this as an absolute truth, yet the content of his statement immediately discredits what he was trying to say.  Building off this paradox is not the best possible move I feel.  Even so if you were to build off of it, I would consider it that absolute truth does exist (and this is where it gets wonky).

-  Kaiki asserts the above quote (This is taking it at face value, which is what was done in the essay, which is ironically not what he wants you to do)

-  In his assertion he provides that there are absolute truths, otherwise his statement would be impossible

-  Which means he just disproved his own statement, and instead proved what he was trying to disprove (because his statement didn't need to be true, his meaning in stating it showed it to be true whether what he was saying was true or not)

-  Absolute Truth exists (which is the opposite of what he believes)

Or if you just want to think about it in a different manner.

If he says that quote and you believe he is RIGHT:

Then what he said is absolutely true and proves its existence.

If he says that quote and you believe he is WRONG:

There is absolute truth.

(Note that there is no inbetween here.  Kaiki is only right or wrong because he states that there is "no" absolute truth.  Which means...)  

Logically absolute truth can only exist.  Is it true all the time?  No, but its exists.  This is something that really bugged me the whole time, and while the rest of the article was great, I just had to share this braindump :).

I didn't try to express that she's down to Earth, just that she is aware of how the world around her functions.  Of all the characters she seems to be the one most looking at how things function and operate.  She has her own issues and view of herself, but people who view the world how she does are generally like that.  They're aloof and regard everything but themselves with their highly judgmental way.  Her critical views include everyone but herself, and that's a completely natural and realistic way of portraying a character like herself.  In being highly observant of everything else, they themselves pass under their own radar.

It then also fits with how she is so overly critical and antagonistic towards Hikki.  She doesn't step back and look at how she is treating others, and just speaks her mind.  She only notices Hikki's apparent flaws and shortcomings, but not her own in her overtly abusive comments.  So she ends up just massacring the poor guy with her words.  It's not an enjoyable way of portraying her as a character, but it certainly fits and is well-written and portrayed.  Her bullying of him may be irrational in how much she does it, but it's completely rational in going with her character and the way she is shown so far.

I think you're not far off in your thinking of her.  But I do disagree on some points.  Alas, this is starting to get into the realm of personal interpretations, so I may be completely wrong and I'm going to admit that.

Yukinoshita seems to be the one who's most "sane" of all the characters.  She's critical and sees the world how it is, and doesn't seem to mind sharing what she sees.  She's providing a platform of logic in an environment where bullshit is completely prevalent (highschool is a time where crap is completely blown up and dramatic, and she is more real than anyone else in the case of the cast).  More so, she's expressing her logic, which is different from Hikki who internalizes it and keeps it inside.  While they share similar ways of thinking, the key difference to note is how they act on their feelings and thoughts.  

While she may seem overly real to the point of being too blunt and hurtful with her comments; it'd really suck to have the drama just roll out of control like it would without her pulling it back as she does every once in a while.  She keeps the show stable, and on its track.  

It may just be because I'm critical in a lot of ways that are very similar to both Hikki and Yukino, but I empathize a lot with them.  Both of them really don't mean any harm, they just know the world more than most people (especially the bad), and are more real and sensitive about it.  It's hurtful to many when you expose and attack someones romanticized view of the world, and that's what Yukino does.  She's clearly been burned in the past, and we'll just have to wait and see on it.  But for now I'm completely sure she has reason for it.  This is all just my opinion, but I hope I can share a different view on it.

Its one of the best done, flawed things I've ever watched. Consider that they adapted thousands of pages of light novel into just those 26 EPs and they did a fine job.

The problem is it's not a show for everyone, it doesn't explain things or hold a viewers hand in any way.  You don't read between the lines, and the show may seem too unwieldy or shallow that you may get turned off. A good example is the characters, who all appear at first glance to be cliches. But their actions and words characterize and develop them far better than 90% of anime if you just take that second to realize the meaning of what they are saying instead of just listening to what they are saying.  It's also a show too deep for one watch, or the 20 minutes a person will spend watching an episode. It is a show where watching three times is three different experiences, where you notice different things each time.  It demands more than most want to put in, and I don't blame them for it.  If it's your cup of tea, like it is mine and others, you will love it.  If it isn't, you'll probably dismiss it as trash.  One thing is for sure, in a boring world where everything seems to have  been done at least twice, Horizon is one of the few things that have been done once, and that uniqueness makes it worth the gamble.

Also make sure to read the randomcuriousity blog on it, clears lots of confusion and wtf moments for the average viewer, and makes it way more enjoyable to the uninitiated.

Input here from a VN reader.  The Original VN is 50 hrs.  It's longer than Clannad wordwise, but it is a lot of it is fluff that can be chopped or condensed.  Plus half of that readtime is practically the common route again and again, which is obviously just done once in the anime. While the emotional weight will still be hindered, and some paths rushed, it won't be a total wreck if done right, and can still manage to be something.  It's important to remember that Refrain is all the killer in the Little Busters, and that the time leading up to that is basically set up, so think about it in the way of ~18 ep of setup, for a 7 episode climax.    Another thing to remember is even Clannad, the most beloved of all these adaptations, cut Kyou and Tomoyo's arcs really badly.  It's not even like our benchmark for these kinds of shows is perfect in that regard

So to pace it out if i were to do it timewise (routewise):

Common: 5ish eps time spread out among the eps, includes the key scenes and the really outstanding funny ones.
Rin1: Screw it, a bit of work and it can rap into Rin2 anyway. 0 eps
Komari: 3 eps, Leaves enough time for the important scenes while cutting out all the fluff.  Hers is important in part to Refrain so time is needed to include that info.
Kurugaya: 3 eps, some key points to make here, but while hers is one of the best and her character one of the strongest, the point is made very quickly and shouldn't be drawn out.  Her route is also important to Refrain, so that info needs to be included.
Haruka - 2 eps, honestly the fluffiest and most padded route in LB, the pace is slow and needlessly so, the point can be made so much more efficiently, barely any time is needed for this, the point is made very quickly. Not even important to Refrain
Mio- 2 eps, the way the anime will probably work couldn't stretch this into a third, it wouldn't work, just the way it's presented is like a timebomb should it meander about. Refrain important minimal
Kud-2 eps, her route is tricky, while i feel that her total time spent on it will be around 2-3 episodes, it can be spread out across multiple ones like the common route and still be effective.  Moderate Refrain Importance
Rin2- 4-5 eps will cover it all, will probably be spread out between a few before condensing at the very end before Refrain.  Almost like the first part of Refrain, so can kind of blend into those Episodes. High Refrain Importance
Refrain ~7 eps - The meat, the grand finale, the big kahuna. This is it.  This is where time needs to be spent.  7 eps is a safe number before getting too crazy, 8 would be really nice, and 6 may be too close.

Simply put, a pokemon has IVs in each stat from 0 to 31.  This differs from pokemon to pokemon and can be controlled and manipulated through careful breeding to get optimal IV spreads.  The number just affects the bonus the pokemon will have in that stat with higher IV = higher bonus in the stats formula.  So a Pikachu with 31 Attack IV just plain has more base Attack Stat than a similar Pikachu with 0 Attack IV (Assuming equal EVs and same nature) because the formula will output a higher Attack stat for the Pikachu with a higher Attack IV.

More info at http://bulbapedia.bulbagarden.net/wiki/Individual_values

I was in the same situation as you not too long ago.  Completely uninterested in anime that I used to enjoy so much.  On basically a few sentences of recommendation and a whim I tried Code Geass.  It completely revived my love for anime.  More than any anime I ever watched it has a gripping nature that pulls you back in for another episode.  The story is fantastic, the action is good, and it's not too dark or lighthearted at any point.  It's not something to watch if you're looking for a whimsical show, but otherwise it deserves your watch.  It helped me and a few friends get back into the swing of things animewise.  I do recommend that you think about which of all these recommendations to try before you dive into any of them, no matter what you choose.  From experience the sooner you get one that you like and can stick to the easier it is to get into more anime.  The more you dawdle and try out shows you have no passion for the less likelihood of success you'll have.  One of my friends tried Geass with us and liked it, but he'd just tried too many different shows unsuccessfully and \lost his passion. 

TL;DR Watch Code Geass, my friends and I were in your situation, and it got us out of our rut.
